text: Some matches are remembered for drama. Late goals, comebacks, controversy.
This one is remembered for something rarer: perfection. For ninety minutes, one of the best teams in the world was made to look like it was playing a different sport.
Barcelona five, Real Madrid nil. The night of the manita — the little hand. This is the story of the match many people still call the best performance of the Guardiola era.
We'll start with the man who came to Madrid specifically to stop this Barça team, and with the plan Guardiola used against him.
Then the five goals, one by one — and the bitter war that followed.
Part one. The challenger.
In April twenty ten, José Mourinho's Inter Milan had knocked Guardiola's Barcelona out of the Champions League semi-finals, defending brilliantly at the Camp Nou with ten men.
A month later, Real Madrid hired Mourinho. The message was clear: this is the man who knows how to beat Barça.
And it was working. When Madrid arrived at the Camp Nou at the end of November, they were top of the league, unbeaten, one point ahead of Barcelona.
On paper, it was the most balanced Clásico in years. Madrid had Cristiano Ronaldo, Mesut Özil, Ángel Di María and a coach who had just won the treble.
Barça had the midfield that had just won the World Cup with Spain: Xavi, Iniesta and Busquets. And they had Messi.
Almost everybody expected a close, tense game.
Part two. The plan.
Guardiola's plan wasn't complicated. Barça would keep the ball through Xavi, Iniesta and Busquets, and use their numbers in midfield to outnumber Madrid's central players.
Messi started in the centre and dropped deep, so Madrid's centre-backs had nobody to mark — and Barça had one more player in the middle of the pitch.
And whenever Barça lost the ball, they had to win it back within seconds. If Madrid never had the ball for long, Ronaldo and Di María could never run.
Part three. The five goals.
Tenth minute. Iniesta slides a pass behind the defence. Xavi, arriving late into the box, takes it with his heel and his knee — and pokes it in. One–nil.
Eighteenth minute. David Villa crosses low from the left, and Pedro finishes at the far post. Two–nil.
After twenty minutes, Madrid had barely touched the ball. Mourinho's team, built to stop Barça, couldn't get near them.
By half-time, the Camp Nou was in a kind of disbelief. This wasn't a close, tense game. It was a lesson.
And in the second half, it got worse for Madrid.
Fifty-fifth minute. Messi, from deep, threads a pass between the Madrid centre-backs. Villa runs onto it and finishes. Three–nil.
Three minutes later, almost the same move. Messi again, a pass through the middle, Villa again. Four–nil.
Messi didn't score that night. He didn't need to. Two passes, two goals, and the whole Madrid defence pulled apart.
And then, in stoppage time, one more. A young substitute from the academy, Jeffrén Suárez, had been on the pitch for barely a minute.
Bojan crossed, and Jeffrén finished. Five–nil.
In the final moments, Sergio Ramos was sent off for a foul on Messi, and a scuffle broke out. It summed up Madrid's night.
In the stands, fans held up five fingers. On the pitch, Gerard Piqué did the same, holding his hand up to the crowd: the manita, the little hand. Five goals.

It was a gesture with history. Barça fans remembered the five–nil at the Bernabéu in nineteen seventy-four. Madrid fans remembered their own five–nil against Barça in nineteen ninety-five. Now it was Barça's turn again.
Part four. Why it was perfect.
Why do people call it perfect? First, the ball. Barça kept it almost all night, and moved it so quickly that Madrid were always chasing.
Second, the press. Every time Madrid won possession, three Barça players surrounded them. They never had time to start a counter-attack.
Third, the academy. Most of the players on the pitch for Barça — Valdés, Piqué, Puyol, Busquets, Xavi, Iniesta, Pedro, Messi, and finally Jeffrén — had come through La Masia.
And fourth, the stage. It happened in a Clásico, against a team that was top of the league, coached by the man hired specifically to stop them.
Part five. The war that followed.

The five–nil didn't end the rivalry. It made it more bitter. In the spring of twenty eleven, the two clubs played each other four times in eighteen days — in the league, the cup final and the Champions League semi-finals. They were some of the angriest games in the rivalry's history.
Madrid won the cup. But Barça won the league.
And in May, at Wembley, they beat Manchester United three–one in the Champions League final — with a performance many people compare to the night of the manita.
Great teams win big games all the time. What made the five–nil different was how it looked.
Against one of the most expensive squads ever assembled, coached by one of the most successful managers in the world, Barça made football look simple. Pass, move, win it back, pass again.
For anyone who watched it, it was the purest version of the idea Cruyff had brought to the club decades earlier. It may never be repeated quite like that again.
Is this the greatest Clásico performance ever? Or does another one beat it? Tell me in the comments.
And for the night eighteen months earlier when this team first announced itself, watch the two–six next.
